title: Camera-based switch-off of Wind turbines with Bird Vision
abstract: Bürgerwindpark Hohenlohe GmbH has developed a technical anti-collision system called BirdVision® for automatic camera-based bird protection. The BirdVision® camera system developed is intended to create a protection concept for wind power-sensitive bird species in wind farms, which provides for a camera-based automatic shutdown in the event of actual hazard situations during periods with an increased probability of collision-prone bird species, such as is the case with field management due to the attraction effect or during phenologyrelated shutdown periods. This approach is intended to take into account the interests of species conservation and the energy transition at the same time. Five Vestas V126-3.3 wind turbines were erected at the Weißbach wind farm (district of Hohenlohe, Baden-Württemberg), which is operated by Bürgerwindpark Hohenlohe GmbH, in 2016. For the Weißbach wind farm, there is a wind farm-specific switch-off policy during field work as an avoidance measure for the red kite. In addition, a demand-orientated shutdown is permitted, which replaces the blanket shutdown. The BirdVision® anti-collision system for automatic camera-based bird protection was developed and tested at the wind farm in order to further optimise the shutdown during field work. Following a monitoring phase, the system was approved for use at the Weißbach wind farm. The system automatically and autonomously stops the wind turbine in question for the period in which collision-sensitive birds (see LUBW 2020/2021) are present in the danger zone of the wind turbine during shutdown-relevant events (e.g. field management). The system is already replacing a blanket shutdown at two wind farms in Baden-Württemberg and is to used in future for other wind farm projects with a wide range of species protection requirements as an avoidance measure to reduce the collision risk of wind power-sensitive bird species. This report summarises the development and functionality of the system.

Bürgerwindpark Hohenlohe GmbH has developed a technical anti-collision system called BirdVision® for automatic camera-based bird protection. The BirdVision® camera system developed is intended to create a protection concept for wind power-sensitive bird species in wind farms, which provides for a camera-based automatic shutdown in the event of actual hazard situations during periods with an increased probability of collision-prone bird species, such as is the case with field management due to the attraction effect or during phenologyrelated shutdown periods. This approach is intended to take into account the interests of species conservation and the energy transition at the same time.

Five Vestas V126-3.3 wind turbines were erected at the Weißbach wind farm (district of Hohenlohe, Baden-Württemberg), which is operated by Bürgerwindpark Hohenlohe GmbH, in 2016. For the Weißbach wind farm, there is a wind farm-specific switch-off policy during field work as an avoidance measure for the red kite. In addition, a demand-orientated shutdown is permitted, which replaces the blanket shutdown. The BirdVision® anti-collision system for automatic camera-based bird protection was developed and tested at the wind farm in order to further optimise the shutdown during field work. Following a monitoring phase, the system was approved for use at the Weißbach wind farm.

The system automatically and autonomously stops the wind turbine in question for the period in which collision-sensitive birds (see LUBW 2020/2021) are present in the danger zone of the wind turbine during shutdown-relevant events (e.g. field management). The system is already replacing a blanket shutdown at two wind farms in Baden-Württemberg and is to used in future for other wind farm projects with a wide range of species protection requirements as an avoidance measure to reduce the collision risk of wind power-sensitive bird species.

This report summarises the development and functionality of the system.

The camera system consists of high-performance industrial cameras equipped with wideangle lenses. A system for a wind turbine  of 6 x 2 cameras (stereo camera sets for distance measurement), which are mounted at the base of the tower of a wind turbine.

are attached to the wind turbine. The mounting height of the system can be adapted to the local conditions. This means that the system can be installed in the forest above treetop level.

A high-performance image processing server with an interface to Fleximaus (Fleximaus GmbH) is installed in the WTG. Fleximaus provides an interface to the WTG for almost all manufacturers. In the event of a dangerous flight, the stop signals generated by BirdVision® are sent to the wind turbine via Fleximaus. Fleximaus also monitors BirdVision® and establishes communication with the turbine. If BirdVision® fails, Fleximaus ensures that the turbine is shut down.

The following figures show a diagram of the camera arrangement on the towers of the wind turbines and the camera sets mounted on the tower at the Weißbach wind farm (Hohenlohe district, Baden-Württemberg).

Various variables can be set for the system on the software side. These variables are used, among other things, to reduce false alarms caused by objects that are not relevant to switching off, such as insects and aeroplanes. If these objects are recognised by the grid defined for these variables, no detections are made and no videos or image data are output and no stop signal is triggered. The variables are flexibly adjustable and can therefore be customised to the respective location where BirdVision® is used. These include the definition of a safety zone around the camera system, within which the system should switch off when birds are detected, or the size classification of detected objects. Possible parameters that can be variably set in the system are listed in Appendix 9.1.

In 2019, the basic version of the BirdVision® camera system was installed on WTG 1 and WTG 3 at the Weißbach wind farm (Hohenlohe district, Baden-Württemberg). WTG 3 is located in open land on a slope. WTG 1 is also located in open land on a slope, but borders a wooded area to the north. The system is intended to protect black kites, red kites and honey buzzards in wind farms. The functionality of the camera system was tested by monitoring in 2019. Automatic switch-off had not yet been implemented at this time.

The system was further developed in 2020. As part of this, an automatic switch-off function and a stereo system for distance measurement were implemented. In addition, further software adjustments were made for bird detection and to prevent false triggering.

For the years 2021 and 2022, the trial use of the camera system at the Weißbach wind farm was approved by the responsible authority for the protection of the red kite at WTG 1 and WTG 3. This means that the camera system can be used in real operation for the first time.

In 2023, the trial use of BirdVision® was extended at the Weißbach wind farm. Monitoring took place at the same time. During the monitoring, a shutdown was implemented according to size classification. BirdVision® was also installed at another wind farm in the forest (Bretzfeld-Obersulm wind farm, Heilbronn district, Baden-Württemberg) to record the flight activity of birds at a forest site.

The use of BirdVision® was approved in another wind farm in 2024 (WTG 1 in the Rote Steige wind farm, Schwäbisch Hall district, Baden-Württemberg) as a replacement for a blanket shutdown for the honey buzzard over defined periods of time (phenology-related shutdown). WTG 1 of the wind farm is located in open land, but is surrounded by forest on three sides or located on the edge of the forest. The system is therefore also installed above tree canopy level.

In addition, the use of the camera system on WTG 4 in the Weißbach wind farm was approved in 2024. WTG 4 is located in open land on a slope, but borders on forest on two sides, which is why the system is installed above tree canopy level.

In addition, a test of the functionality of the system was carried out in 2024 at a wind farm in Lower Saxony (wind turbines are located in open land) using a test framework from Schleswig-Holstein.

During the test phase of the on-demand shutdown (manual shutdown using web-based software from Vestas ("Vestas Online Enterprise") via tablet) in 2017, the distance at which a bird of prey detection is required for the Vestas V126-3.3 turbine was tested on 18 dates at the Weißbach wind farm (Hohenlohe district, Baden- Württemberg) to ensure that the turbine is stopped in good time and no longer poses a risk to the bird. This was checked when using the demand-based shutdown in the years 2018 - 2022. A manually switched off Vestas V126-3.3 WTG comes to a standstill (in strong winds) within a maximum of 30-35 seconds and then no longer poses a collision risk for birds at risk of collision. In light and moderate winds, the time until the rotors come to a standstill is correspondingly shorter. In addition, a wind turbine normally no longer poses a risk to bird species at risk of collision even before the rotor blades come to a standstill, as soon as the rotor blade speed  only low and no longer significantly higher than the spin speed. In average winds, this is the case after a maximum of 15-20 seconds, meaning that the risk of collision can normally be averted very quickly.

During an autonomous shutdown by the BirdVision® camera system at the Weißbach wind farm (Vestas V 126-3.3), the same duration was recorded until the corresponding WTG rotors came to a standstill. During test operation on WTG 1 at the Rote

Steige (district of Schwäbisch Hall, Baden-Württemberg), comparable times were observed until the rotor blades on the Vestas V136 wind turbine came to a standstill.

The flight movements relevant to shutdown are mainly food-seeking birds of prey that search the ground for food in comparatively slow flight curves or circling. Within the defined danger zone of 200 metres, the turbines can be switched to standstill or spin mode in good time before an actual hazard situation arises. This was tested during the monitoring dates and was confirmed. A greater distance of 300 m as a danger zone led to a significantly higher number of shutdowns, without a significantly higher level of protection being achieved, as the detected birds in the area between 200 - 300 m around the turbine location either did not fly closer to the WTGs or the turbines switched to spin mode in good time even after detection within a 200 m radius around the WTGs, so that there was no longer a risk of collision.

In the wind farms where the system is used, the danger zone was agreed and defined with the responsible authority based on the observations and test operation. This was mainly due to the fact that the rotor blades of a turbine in spin mode no longer have a collision risk speed.

To validate the system, a relatively high number of monitoring dates were generally carried out in 2019 - 2022 (see Table 1). While monitoring was predominantly carried out in good weather conditions, monitoring was also carried out on five rainy days in 2019 to test the functionality of the cameras in unfavourable weather conditions and limited visibility.

In 2023, a test operation place at the Rote Steige wind farm, during which employees of the responsible approval authority were able to examine the functionality of the camera system on site. At the same time, monitoring for BirdVision® took place.

The monitoring focussed in particular on the red kite, black kite and honey buzzard species, which are relevant to the shutdown in accordance with legal requirements.

As the use of the camera system at the Weißbach wind farm has already been approved for two WTGs, only two appointments were required for WTG 4 in accordance with the approval in order to check the functionality of the system before it was used. As the use of BirdVision® was approved for the first time at the Rote Steige wind farm, two dates were scheduled to test the functionality and at least five additional monitoring dates before the system was used.

Monitoring was terminated prematurely twice in total due to a lack of flight activity. Of these, monitoring was terminated prematurely once in 2019 during rainy weather. Monitoring was terminated once again in 2024 at the Rote Steige wind farm in favourable weather conditions but in the absence of flight activity.

Locations were chosen as observation points (fixed points) for the monitoring from which the 200 m to approx. 500 m radius around the respective plant could be easily seen.

The monitoring dates generally took place on days with suitable flight conditions for birds at risk of collision. Monitoring was carried out for at least three hours on each date. Monitoring was terminated prematurely on a total of two dates. These two dates were nevertheless  in the analysis. During this time, the flight routes, dwell time, flight behaviour and flight altitude birds of prey at risk of collision (red kite, black kite, honey buzzard, peregrine falcon, etc.) and other birds of prey (common buzzard, kestrel) were recorded within a 200 m to 200 m radius.

In some cases, a professionally trained person noted the flight movements on maps within a radius of approx. 500 metres and recorded the duration of the flight movements. Other birds such as songbirds, pigeons, etc. are not classified as relevant to switching off and were categorised as false triggering of the camera system. With the introduction of the size classification from 2023, falcons were also categorised as not relevant for shutdown due to the size classification for the monitored wind farms.

At the same time, a second person used a laptop to view live recordings from the installed cameras (BirdVision®) on the corresponding wind turbines via a remote connection during the monitoring process, so that an initial live comparison between field observations and camera recordings was already possible in the field. At the same time, it was possible check whether an automatic switch-off was triggered in good time if necessary. Subsequently, the camera recordings (video recordings and image data) and log files for the automatic shutdown of the wind turbines for the monitoring period were analysed for each monitoring date. The individual video recordings/image data were checked for false triggering and bird detection and, as far as possible, assigned to the individual flight movements observed in the field.

The 200 m radius around the respective WTG was used as the basis for the monitoring analyses. The 200 m radius was defined as a danger zone for birds at risk of collision at the wind farms where monitoring was carried out (see Chapter 4). If a bird of prey moves within the defined radius, the turbine is ideally switched off automatically.

As the automatic shutdown by means of the camera system for the individual WTGs in the wind farms monitored is limited to the detection of flight movements within a 200 m radius, only flight movements within a 200 m radius of the respective WTG were taken into account. Flight movements at an altitude of well over 200 m that did not trigger a stop signal were also not taken into account, as these do not represent hazardous flights.

The factors that were included in the evaluation or classified as irrelevant are listed below.

Factors that are not relevant for switching off are

- Flight movement outside the 200 m radius

- Aircraft movements at a height of well over 200 m and therefore no longer in the danger zone of the wind turbines

- Bird detections not relevant to switching off (pigeons, corvids, skylarks, etc.)

- Shutdown-relevant birds sitting on the ground

The statistics continue to include

- Aircraft movements within the 200 m radius that were detected but for which an alarm had not triggered a stop signal

- Technical causes (system crash etc.)

The monitoring in 2019 took place exclusively to validate the camera system. The output of stop signals for corresponding flight movements was not yet implemented at this time. The results from 2019 are therefore not taken into account. No monitoring took place in 2020. This means that the monitoring results to date will only be analysed from 2021 onwards. The results of the monitoring for the Weißbach wind farm and the Rote Steige wind farm were used for the analysis. Only the flight movements within the 200 m radius were taken into account when analysing the monitoring, as this area was defined as a danger zone for the wind farms in question. Until 2023, kestrels were still included in the evaluation as relevant for shutdown, as they were not categorised according to size. Thereafter, due to the size categorisation as "small" for the tested system, as there are no falcon species classified as sensitive to wind power (tree falcon, peregrine falcon) in the tested wind farms that are comparable in size to kestrels. The following diagram shows the evaluation of bird detection from 2021 to 2024.

Thanks to the continuous further development of the system, the detection rate and the protection rate of flight movements of relevant large birds within a 200 m radius of the respective wind turbine could be continuously improved.

In 2021 and 2022, flight movements at the edge of the 200 m radius in particular, which only had very short flight sequences within the 200 m radius, did not lead to an automatic stop. This was regulated in subsequent years with the further development of the system and the adjusted setting of the filter options.

Furthermore, very low flight movements (approx. 0-30 m flight altitude above the ground) or those just above the treetops did not lead to an automatic stop of the WTG, as these were not recognised by the system due to the lack of contrast with the background. However, such low flight movements do not usually lead to actual danger situations for the relevant birds, as there is still a relatively large distance to the rotor area and the flight movement is detected as soon as the bird flies a little higher again. Furthermore, no low flight movements were observed during the entire observation period in which the bird abruptly lost altitude.

and therefore could not  been switched off by the camera system in time.

Flight movements did not lead to a stop were also categorised incorrectly in some cases. On the software side, the size categorisation is being continuously developed in order to further optimise this function.

Various causes of false detections that triggered stop signals were identified during the monitoring. These included aircraft/helicopters, smaller birds not classified as sensitive to wind power according to LUBW, such as skylarks, pigeons and corvids, insects or other turbines and sun/clouds. The following illustration shows the false detections broken down according to the reason for triggering.

In 2021, 35 % of the stop signals were false detections. In 2022, stop signals in particular from birds not considered to be at risk of collision, such as

skylarks, pigeons, corvids, etc., led to an increased switch-off rate due to false detections of 74 %. In the following years 2023 and 2024, stop signals due to false detections were reduced to 31 % and 35 % respectively. However, it should also be noted here that false triggering is heavily dependent on the location (open land, forest, forest edge, etc.) and the detection period.

Due to the high proportion of stop signals from birds not classified as at risk of collision (e.g. skylarks, pigeons, corvids, etc.) during the first two monitoring years 2021 and 2022, tests were carried out with software-adjustable variables. In the tested system, the minimum distance for triggering a stop signal within the safety zone was therefore increased to 30 m in order to prevent stop signals from flights of small birds in the vicinity of the WTG. In addition, a further adjustable variable for the system was further developed in 2023. This is the categorisation of the object size, which is divided into four categories ("small", "medium", "large" and

"huge") is issued. Falcons, corvids, other songbirds (e.g. skylark), pigeons etc. are categorised as "small" in the tested system. When this function is activated, the system no longer triggers a stop for objects categorised as "small". As a result, false triggering of stop signals for birds that are not relevant for switching off, such as skylarks and pigeons, could be significantly reduced.

Aeroplanes and helicopters also led to more frequent shutdowns of the wind turbines, which is why the "huge" category was included in the size classification of objects. Aircraft are in this category if this function is activated in the system. Due to this categorisation, it was not possible to switch off the system due to aircraft or helicopters can be reduced.

During the first monitoring dates, it was also observed that insects were frequently detected, although they rarely triggered a stop signal. To reduce the detection of insects, the so-called "insect filter" was activated. This defines a minimum distance to the camera. If the distance falls below the minimum distance, no image and video data is generated and the flight movement does not cause the system to switch off. This successfully prevented the detection of insects during the subsequent monitoring sessions.

Based on several years of monitoring the BirdVision® camera system, extensive experience has been gained regarding the functionality of the system. The system has also been continuously developed further. In view of the experience gained to date, the following criteria are recommended for the use of the camera system (during shutdown-relevant events) to minimise the collision risk at wind turbines for commissioning and subsequent years:

To summarise, it should be noted that bird detections also occur far beyond the 200 m radius around the WTGs. In the vast majority of casesflight movements in the defined danger zone result in an automatic shutdown of the WTG. In the case of flight movements that last longer than 3 minutes in the danger zone, the

rule, a repeated stop signal is sent, which leads to an extension of the stop signal by a further 3 minutes.

From version 2.9.0.1 of BirdVision®, it is now possible to switch off depending on the size classification of objects. The function can be switched on or off as required and was activated for test purposes during monitoring in 2023 and used in 2024. By further optimising the size classification, subsequent versions of BirdVision® will improve the categorisation of birds or detected objects by size so that incorrect classifications can be further reduced.

Due to the good detection and protection rate of the camera system with automatic switchoff, experts believe that the use of the BirdVision® camera system during switch-off-relevant events (e.g. field processing, phenology-related switch-off) is suitable for significantly reducing the collision risk of wind power-sensitive bird species such as the red kite and honey buzzard.

For the use of BirdVision® as an avoidance measure for bird species at risk of collision, monitoring should carried out to check the functionality of WTGs equipped with BirdVision®. In addition, the duration from the output of the stop signal to the standstill of the rotors should be checked for the WTGs where BirdVision® is to be used in order to adjust the danger zone if necessary.

- Definition of the safety zone:

- The safety zone setting is used to specify the range within which a flying object will trigger an alarm and thus a stop signal to the WTG. It is possible to set both a minimum and a maximum distance. The minimum distance specifies the minimum distance the object must be from the camera in order to  an alarm and thus a stop signal ( ⇒ was set to 30 metres in the tested system in order to prevent stop signals from being triggered by flights of small birds in the vicinity of the WTG).

The maximum distance specifies the distance from the camera up to which an alarm and therefore a stop is triggered.

Objects that  detected at a greater distance do not trigger an alarm and therefore do not stop the WTG ( ⇒ specified as 200 m in the tested system). The safety zone in the tested system is therefore 30 - 200 m from the respective camera. Birds detected within this range that fulfil the minimum duration of stay within the zone are recognised as a dangerous flight, a stop signal is sent and the WTG is consequently stopped.
